newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trustbuster cautious on defense mergers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trustbuster cautious on defense mergers.

text.p: Trustbuster Robert Pitofsky, whose Federal Trade Commission will review the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger, signaled a note of caution Thursday about the wave of defense industry consolidations, saying they must "halt somewhere."
"As long as there were three or four firms left, downsizing makes great sense," Pitofsky, who chairs the FTC, told Reuters in an interview.

"When there are only two left or when there's only one left, then -- both from the point of view of the Pentagon protecting its own interests and from the point of view of the antitrust laws protecting the taxpayers' interest -- you've got to call a halt somewhere," he said.

The FTC has jurisdiction to halt mergers if they create monopolies or eliminate competition, but so far it has approved one multibillion-dollar defense industry merger after another, although sometimes it has restructured them.
"I think what's happened up until now makes great sense," said Pitofsky, "There was vast overcapacity in the industry."
The FTC will review the proposed $15 billion merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp., which is also being actively checked at the Pentagon.

Boeing produces mostly commercial aircraft and its military capacity mostly complements that of McDonnell Douglas. Analysts say the FTC will take a close look, weapons system by weapons system, to see what competitors remain.

Either the FTC or the Justice Department will scrutinize the recently proposed sale of Hughes Electronics to Raytheon Co.. That came after Raytheon acquired the defense electronics unit of Texas Instruments Inc..

Pitofsky's new questions about defense mergers come shortly after senior defense officials expressed concern that rapid consolidation of the defense industry and a shrinking military budget could create problems in obtaining some spare parts, especially for older weapons.

William Cohen, who will be sworn in as the new defense secretary at the White House on Friday, said in written testimony to the Senate Armed Services Committee this week that "we may have lost something in the process" of industrial mergers.

"We clearly have less opportunity for competition in many defense sectors, and that means we will have to develop new acquisition strategies to insure best value for the government," Cohen said. But he continued to endorse defense mergers, so long as they increase efficiency and save taxpayers' money.
The deals which have been approved so far by the FTC have been huge.

For example, Lockheed merged with Martin Marietta in November 1995 in a deal worth $9 billion and acquired Loral Corp. the following spring for $9.1 billion. Boeing purchased Rockwell's space business last month for $3 billion, and Litton Industries Inc. purchased PRC Inc. from Black and Decker Corp. in February 1996 for $425 million.
The FTC has reviewed all of the major mergers among aerospace companies in recent years. The Pentagon advises the FTC on the mergers but has no role in the final decision.
